architect.rationale: Diamond, because the slices meet all three conditions. (a) After s1 there are three slices with disjoint files: s2 owns orchestrad/src/config.rs; s3 owns orchestrad/src/control.rs and qr.rs; s5 owns orchestrad/systemd/*, README.md, config.example.toml, tests/unit_file.rs, .github/workflows/test.yml, CLAUDE.md and protocol/README.md. s4 owns main.rs, daemon.rs, log.rs, preflight.rs and tests/daemon.rs. The shared files every module needs (orchestrad/Cargo.toml, src/lib.rs with all module declarations, the root Cargo.toml and Cargo.lock) belong to s1 alone, and every dependency is declared there, so no later slice touches the lockfile. (b) Each done_when runs alone: config:: and control::/qr:: unit tests, a unit-file pin test, and a cross-target cargo check --target x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu (target already installed), so a Windows builder proves Linux code at least compiles. (c) It is a network-facing service run as a system user, which I would not merge unreviewed. orchestra is a git repo, so each slice gets its own branch. Edges are real: s1 makes the crate, addr.rs and host.rs that everything compiles against. s4 consumes the Config from s2 and the Handler, client and QR from s3. s5 needs only the crate (for its test target) and the CLI surface fixed in this plan, so it runs in parallel with s2-s4. Core-vs-duplicate: MOVE where mechanical. The address rules (classify, port_error, ports) and the boot sequence (store/transcripts/worktrees/Sessions/restore/pump) move into core and the desktop calls them. The rules are pure, and the boot sequence is the same 25 lines both hosts would otherwise copy. Do NOT move the desktop config.json loader: its schema (enabled, firewall_notice_seen, read-only fallback, adapter enumeration via if-addrs) is desktop policy, and the orchestrad file has other fields and a different failure rule (refuse to start). The QR stays per binary (SVG for the webview, unicode for a terminal), and qrcode stays out of core. A new crate rather than core/src/bin: it keeps qrcode/toml out of the engine deps, and the CI cost (one test line) is paid in s5. Platform: orchestrad behaviour is cfg(target_os=linux), not unix, because SO_PEERCRED and PR_* are Linux-only, so the macOS core check is unaffected. Windows builds a stub main and runs the pure tests. Risk tags: s1 high, because it edits desktop lib.rs and link_config.rs, whose semantics must not change, and it owns the shared Cargo/lib.rs files. s2 high, because it is the only gate between a text file and a network listener (0.0.0.0, mapped forms, port range), and a wrong low there is an exposure. s3 high, because it carries the pairing secret to a terminal and owns the peer-uid check, which a Windows test cannot run. s4 high, because the secret never reaching the journal and never running as root are properties a test samples but cannot fully see, and most of s4 runs only in Linux CI. s5 low: no secret, no file shared with another slice, the security directives are pinned by a test, and the prose is human-read.

plan.intent: orchestrad config file: parse and validate, pure, no I/O except reading the one path. Format (TOML if G1 holds): schema = 1; optional host_name; [link] port (default 47800, core port_error 1024-65535, never 0) and binds (IPv4 only, each passing core classify, never 0.0.0.0 or ::ffff:0.0.0.0, at most 16, deduped); [limits] max_connections (1..=16, may only lower the product cap; G3); [[projects]] path (absolute, no '..' component). plan.intent: The local control channel and the terminal QR. control.rs: line-delimited JSON requests and replies (Status, OpenPairing, NextPairingRequest, Confirm{id}, Reject{id}, ClosePairing, ListClients, Revoke{id}), with encode/decode pure and tested everywhere. Under cfg(target_os=linux) it adds a UnixListener server that takes a Handler trait object, so it knows nothing of the daemon, plus a client. The socket path is --socket, else $RUNTIME_DIRECTORY/control.sock (systemd), else $XDG_RUNTIME_DIR/orchestrad/control.sock. The socket is created with umask 0077 / mode 0600. Every accepted peer is checked with SO_PEERCRED and refused unless its uid is the daemon's euid. Each request and reply line is capped at 64 KiB. qr.rs: offer text -> a terminal string using qrcode's unicode Dense1x2 renderer, EcLevel M, quiet zone, with an error for a payload too big for a code.

s1.$comment: RE-REVIEWS NEST, and this is the rule every reader follows. The TOP LEVEL of reviews.<slice> IS attempt 1. A re-review writes attempt_2, then attempt_3, and so on, each with the same fields as the top level. Every attempt SURVIVES PERMANENTLY - history is never overwritten, flattened, or migrated up. The LATEST attempt supplies the verdict: that is what close-run.py, brief.py and verify-state.py resolve through, and what fleetview's finalVerdict() has always shown. `ever_rejected` - did ANY attempt REJECT - is DISPLAY ONLY, forever, so a rejection stays visible after it is fixed; it must never gate anything, or the fleet stops being able to loop. NO NODE MAY REWRITE AN EARLIER ATTEMPT: a second reviewer writes its own attempt_N and leaves the ones before it alone, top-level verdict included - relocating that verdict would destroy the history the board keeps and leave a key stamped written_by:reviewer with someone else as its real author. The KEY INDEX numbers an attempt, not the `attempt` field inside it; the field is display. An EMPTY attempt_N is not a re-review, it is a key nobody wrote - write the whole attempt or none of it. The walk STOPS AT THE FIRST GAP, so an attempt_3 with no attempt_2 is ignored and the earlier verdict stands: A GAP IS MALFORMED AND NO NODE MAY LEAVE ONE. Write the next UNUSED N and never skip - a mis-numbered re-review is not reported anywhere, it is simply unread, and a REJECT nobody reads is a REJECT nobody acts on. The cap is attempt_9, matching fleetview's `for (i = 2; i < 10; i++)` exactly so the two readers cannot disagree; attempt_10 and beyond is reported loudly and resolved by nobody.
